newsitem.title: USA: U.S. insists NATO-Russia deal still unresolved.
newsitem.headline: U.S. insists NATO-Russia deal still unresolved.

text.p: U.S. officials on Thursday insisted a NATO-Russia security agreement is anything but concluded and expressed puzzlement that Russian leaders have publicly acted as if a signing ceremony on May 27 was certain.

They were speaking after President Boris Yeltsin, apparently gambling on the support of his friend and ally Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said after talks in Germany that Russia would clinch an elusive deal with NATO next month.
After a day of talks in the spa resort of Baden-Baden, Yeltsin and Kohl said German influence could break a deadlock between Moscow and the alliance over NATO's eastward expansion.
But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns insisted: "Negotiations have not yet been completed, and so we can't cite a victory before we have it."
Although "we certainly have the hope" there will be agreement on a NATO-Russia charter, he said, "I can't point you to any dramatic progress recently."

"It's obviously good to see that Chancellor Kohl and President Yeltsin had a good discussion on this. And we hope very much that the optimism at the press conference today will be turned into reality in the substance of the negotiations," he added.
Another senior U.S. official told Reuters: "The Russians are, for some reason I don't entirely understand, talking about this as if it were agreed."
"We're not there yet ... There are unresolved issues."

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, added: "It's agreed notionally and provisionally that if we have a NATO-Russia document we'd be prepared to sign it on the 27th but there's a lot of work to be done."

The proposed Russia-NATO charter was aimed at easing Moscow's fears about alliance plans to decide its first new post-Cold War members at a July summit in Madrid. Top contenders are Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
NATO leaders, especially Washington, are unwilling to concede to Russian demands that they say would consign new members to "second-class" NATO participation.
Moscow has demanded that NATO not advance nuclear and other weapons into new member states and insisted on a say in NATO planning based on consensus decisions.
NATO has refused to grant Russia treaty-like guarantees that would have to be ratified by NATO parliaments.

But the alliance has repeatedly stated it has no plans, intention or reason to station nuclear weapons in new NATO member states. The alliance has also said it has no plans to build up conventional forces on Russia's borders.

Asked about these issues anew, Burns cited NATO's earlier statements and said: "I don't see that NATO is going to deviate from its position at all, on either nuclear weapons or the stationing of conventional forces."

The other senior U.S. official told Reuters differences remain with Russia over details for a joint Russia-NATO council in which Moscow would have a voice but no veto on alliance decisions on European security issues.

But he said: "The big issues are on the military side and in reconciling what may be irreconcilable in the end: NATO's absolutely rock-solid position that whether the alliance has 16 members, 19 members or 25 members, all members are equal and the alliance is sovereign.

"Russia's concern is that the alliance not threaten the national security of Russia. I happen to think ... there's a way of reconciling ... our insistence and their need, but it isn't easy and there's a lot of work still to be done and I'm not sure that we'll have it before May 27," he said.
